newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein denies giving detonator to U.S. group.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein denies giving detonator to U.S. group.

text.p: Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, denied on Sunday allegations that it supplied a detonator to a man linked to a U.S. white supremacist group that defence lawyers suggest may have been involved in the Oklahoma City bombing.
Mairead Keane, head of Sinn Fein's Washington office, said in a statement issued in Belfast, Northern Ireland, that the claim was nonsense.
"Any student of the Anglo-Irish conflict will treat as absurd the claims of an Iraqi/US neo-Nazi/white supremacist and Irish Republican conspiracy," Keane said.
Sinn Fein is the political wing of the Irish Republican Army, which is fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland and unite it with the Irish republic.
Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams said the allegation was "preposterous rubbish." "I would be totally dismissive of this sort of silly season story," he told reporters at a Belfast rally.

The allegation was contained in a 155-page court document filed last week by lawyers for U.S. Gulf War veteran Timothy McVeigh, who goes on trial in Denver on Monday charged with blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995.
The blast, the worst attack on U.S. soil, killed 168 people and injured more than 500.

McVeigh's lawyers wanted a federal appeals court to order the U.S. government to turn over classified intelligence data the defence believes may show that international terrorists planned the bombing. The appeals court denied the request on Friday.

In the document, McVeigh's lawyers laid out a complicated hypothesis that a foreign power, probably Iraq, planned an attack in the United States and that one of the targets was the Oklahoma City federal building.

The lawyers theorised that the foreign operatives recruited American neo-Nazis to carry out the bombing and said they may have found the "desired ideology" in Elohim City, Oklahoma, "a small compound...consisting of between 25 and 30 families and described as a terrorist organisation which preaches white supremacy, polygamy and overthrow of the government."

The defence said a paid informant who infiltrated Elohim City told the government before April 19, 1995, that Andreas Strassmeir, a German national who used to live at Elohim City, proposed to bomb federal buildings.

The document said the informant, Carol Howe, told a defence source she had briefed her ATF handler "about the detonator that Andy Strassmeir received from Sinn Fein," which McVeigh's lawyers referred to as "the Irish terrorist group."
The defence document did not allege that the detonator was used in the Oklahoma City bombing. Strassmeir's attorney has denied that his client had any connection with the bombing.
Joseph Hartzler, lead prosecutor in the Oklahoma City case, derided the defence theory last week as "pulp fiction". He said in a court filing it "reads like a bad Hollywood script."
